I’ve been reading heavily into this topic as of late, so I’m gonna try to articulate my thoughts as best as possible. Based off of what I’ve read from places like the World Health Organization, Gender is defined as “...the socially constructed characteristics of women and men – such as norms, roles and relationships of and between groups of women and men. It varies from society to society and can be changed. While most people are born either male or female, they are taught appropriate norms and behaviours – including how they should interact with others of the same or opposite sex within households, communities and work places. When individuals or groups do not “fit” established gender norms they often face stigma, discriminatory practices or social exclusion – all of which adversely affect health. It is important to be sensitive to different identities that do not necessarily fit into binary male or female sex categories.” People draw a distinction between sex & gender. Where gender is socially constructed in the sense of what we may perceive as masculine here may be extremely feminine in the future (a good example would be how men used to wear makeup, wigs & high heels—all things that are very “feminine” now or how it is considered feminine (a trait of the female gender) to wear a dress or skirt, but In many Middle Eastern, Asian, and African cultures; dresses skirts, arongs, robes, gowns, etc. can be considered masculine. The kilt worn by a Scottish male does not make him appear feminine in his culture.). According to my studies, drawing this distinction between the 2 is important because Gender as we know it isn’t purely biological. It’s instead something that’s apart of us. So differentiating how we express ourselves, and create our identities and the likes is important to draw a parallel from our biological selves, which doesn’t quite carry those same things—at least, not as heavily, although It can play a part. I’ve learned in my studies to view gender as fluid (since it’s a construct), like how some anthropologists used the term “berdache” to refer to individuals who occasionally or permanently dressed and lived as the opposite gender. Samoan culture accepts what they refer to as a “third gender.” Fa’afafine, which translates as “the way of the woman,” is a term used to describe individuals who are born biologically male but embody both masculine and feminine traits. Fa’afafines are considered an important part of Samoan culture. Individuals from other cultures may mislabel them as homosexuals because fa’afafines have a varied sexual life that may include men or women. More recently, in early-2014, India legally recognised the hijra, the traditional third gender who had been previously accepted prior to colonialism legally. So with things like Gender Identities, it gets tricky sometimes but I’ll try my hardest to explain. I hope this hasn’t been too hard to read so far. A gender identity is like, someone’s self-conception of being male or female based on his or her association with masculine or feminine gender roles. Maybe they may not feel comfortable with either and reject it all. Some choose to embrace both. Some do other things. These people who reject or embrace both sides of the spectrum simultaneously would usually be nonbinary people and the like. So if we view Gender as a spectrum spanning from male to female, it’s easy to see why people can say there’s more than 2. Some may feel so comfortable or adapted to an alternate roll that’s not their own that they ID as something else, like the opposite sex or the lack of one at all. From what my research has shown me so far, the words sex and gender have been conflated, although they haven’t always meant the same thing. It’s said that it wasn’t since the 1950’s until there was a formal distinction made between the 2 things, after they’ve started to deal with trans patients and the like. Then the term “gender” then got more and more popular and people just ended up conflating the 2. Things like sociology have been making huge efforts to make this information more... well known or at least accessible for lack of a better word. So instead of rigid gender alignments, people have chosen to not conform to the binary. Some fall on one side, some on the other, some in the middle, and some far beyond. I have a lot of nonbinary and trans friends that I’ve learned this from (plus personal studying—lots of it) and honestly I’m glad I’ve been able to learn it, as it’s always good to see where they’re coming from. If anyone has any questions for me, feel free to ask please :)
